title: Blog Post 2
text:
America’s most famous national parks can also be its busiest. A traveler who values open space might ask: Which established parks in the contiguous United States combine substantial visitation with relatively low visitor pressure? Rather than naming my favorite park, I will build a transparent shortlist from two measurable quantities: annual recreation visits and park area.
My metric is annual visits per 1,000 acres. A smaller number means more park acreage relative to recorded visits. It is a screening tool—not a literal count of people someone will meet. Visitors cluster at popular trails, arrive in different seasons, and may enter the same park more than once.

title: Blog Post 2
text:
One respectful request
I scraped the Wikipedia list of U.S. national parks on September 20, 2026. Its table reports 2023 acreage and 2025 recreation visits, citing National Park Service sources. Wikipedia text is available under CC BY-SA 4.0, and this post attributes and links the source rather than copying its prose or images. I also checked Wikipedia’s robots.txt: this ordinary article path is not disallowed. The analysis sends one request, accesses no login or restricted page, and does not crawl individual park pages.
As a provenance check, I compared the scraped leaders with the official NPS Annual Visitation by Park report. The 2025 totals match exactly: Death Valley 1,320,134, Everglades 778,198, and Big Bend 568,104. These are recreation visits, not unique people. The NPS portal remains the appropriate place to verify later revisions before booking.


Show reproducible R code
library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

url <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_parks_of_the_United_States"

# One HTTP request; select the first table by its semantic CSS class.
page <- read_html(url)
raw <- page |>
  html_element("table.wikitable") |>
  html_table(fill = TRUE)

# Footnote numbers in column names can change, so locate columns by prefix.
area_col <- names(raw)[str_detect(names(raw), "^Area")][1]
visit_col <- names(raw)[str_detect(names(raw), "^Recreation visitors")][1]
stopifnot(!is.na(area_col), !is.na(visit_col))

parks <- raw |>
  transmute(
    park = Name |>
      str_remove_all("[†‡*]") |>
      str_squish(),
    location = Location |>
      str_remove("\\s*\\.mw-parser.*$") |>
      str_remove("\\s+\\d.*$") |>
      str_squish(),
    area_acres = parse_number(.data[[area_col]]),
    visits_2025 = parse_number(.data[[visit_col]])
  ) |>
  mutate(visits_per_1000_acres = visits_2025 / (area_acres / 1000))

# Fail loudly if the page structure or numeric parsing has broken.
stopifnot(nrow(parks) >= 60,
          all(!is.na(parks$area_acres)),
          all(!is.na(parks$visits_2025)),
          all(parks$area_acres > 0),
          all(parks$visits_2025 > 0))

# Archive the snapshot this post was built from, so the numbers reported here
# stay reproducible even after Wikipedia is edited.
write_csv(parks, "data/parks_clean.csv")


The scrape returns 63 parks. Separating extraction from cleaning makes the workflow auditable: html_table() collects text; parse_number() removes commas, units, and footnotes; and the checks stop the analysis instead of silently producing nonsense if the page changes.

title: Blog Post 2
text:
Define a useful comparison set
Huge, remote Alaskan parks naturally have very low density but may not suit an ordinary road trip. I therefore exclude Alaska, Hawaii, and U.S. territories, then require at least 500,000 annual visits. The threshold is a simple proxy for an established destination, not a quality judgment. Changing it changes the choice set, so I report it explicitly.


Show reproducible R code
candidates <- parks |>
  filter(
    !str_detect(location, "Alaska|Hawaii|American Samoa|Virgin Islands"),
    visits_2025 >= 500000
  ) |>
  arrange(visits_per_1000_acres)

shortlist <- candidates |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  transmute(
    Park = park,
    Location = location,
    `2025 visits` = scales::comma(visits_2025),
    `Area (acres)` = scales::comma(round(area_acres)),
    `Visits per 1,000 acres` = scales::number(
      visits_per_1000_acres, accuracy = 1
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  shortlist,
  align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = "Lowest visitor pressure among established contiguous-U.S. candidates."
)

title: Blog Post 2
text:
What the comparison reveals


Show reproducible R code
top_eight <- candidates |> slice_head(n = 8)
reference_density <- median(candidates$visits_per_1000_acres)

ggplot(candidates, aes(area_acres, visits_2025)) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = reference_density / 1000,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed", color = "#8A8A8A"
  ) +
  geom_point(color = "#9CB9C8", size = 2.6, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = top_eight, color = "#C4512D", size = 3) +
  geom_text(
    data = top_eight,
    aes(label = park),
    nudge_y = 0.10,
    check_overlap = TRUE,
    size = 3.2,
    color = "#5B2B1E"
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(
    x = "Park area (acres, log scale)",
    y = "2025 recreation visits (log scale)",
    title = "Large parks can absorb the same annual visitation differently",
    subtitle = "Candidates are contiguous-U.S. parks with at least 500,000 visits"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title.position = "plot")








Figure 1: Parks above the dashed line have more visits per 1,000 acres. Labels identify the eight lowest-pressure candidates; both axes are logarithmic so large and small parks remain visible.





Death Valley, Everglades, and Big Bend form the strongest initial shortlist. Death Valley has the lowest ratio in the filtered set: about 387 visits per 1,000 acres. By comparison, the candidate median is about 7,655. Everglades and Big Bend also combine more than half a million visits with large areas. For someone prioritizing space, I would investigate these three before defaulting to the most visited names.

title: Blog Post 2
text:
From ranking to action
The recommendation is to use this shortlist as stage one, then consult official park pages for road access, reservation rules, weather, closures, and seasonal visitation. For example, vast acreage can be wilderness, water, or otherwise inaccessible; annual totals cannot reveal congestion at one entrance at noon. The dataset counts visits rather than unique people and mixes two reference years (2023 area and 2025 visits). Wikipedia can also change after this post is rendered.
Those limitations do not make the analysis useless. They define what it can support: a low-cost way to narrow 63 possibilities, followed by local research. A stronger second stage would scrape or download monthly NPS visitation and compare the traveler’s intended month. That could distinguish a genuinely quieter trip window from a park that only looks spacious in an annual average.






ImportantActionable takeaway



For a crowd-averse contiguous-U.S. park trip, begin with Death Valley, Everglades, and Big Bend, then verify season, access, and conditions with the NPS. The main analytical lesson is equally practical: rank options with a transparent denominator, state the filters, and never mistake acreage-adjusted annual visits for the experience at a particular trail or time.

title: Blog Post 1
text:
Suppose a coin lands heads 7 times in 10 independent flips. The unknown probability of heads is (p). It is tempting to say, “the probability that (p=0.7) is largest.” That sentence quietly confuses probability with likelihood.
Probability reasons forward: if (p) were known, how probable would the data be? For (K(n,p)),

\Pr(K=k\mid p)=\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}.

Likelihood reverses what varies. After observing (k), the data are fixed and candidate values of (p) are compared:

L(p\mid k,n)=\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}, \qquad 0\le p\le 1.

The formula is identical, but its role is different. As a function of (k), it is a probability distribution when (p) is fixed. As a function of (p), it is a likelihood when (k) is fixed. A likelihood need not sum or integrate to one over parameter values. Therefore, (L(0.7)) is not ((p=0.7K=7)); a probability distribution for (p) requires additional assumptions, such as a Bayesian prior.

title: Blog Post 1
text:
Comparing candidate coins
Because likelihoods can be extremely small, it is useful to divide every value by the largest one. This creates a relative likelihood whose maximum is 1 without changing which (p) fits best.


Show reproducible R code
n <- 10
k <- 7

candidate_p <- c(0.30, 0.50, 0.70, 0.90)
candidate_loglik <- dbinom(k, size = n, prob = candidate_p, log = TRUE)
candidate_relative <- exp(candidate_loglik - max(candidate_loglik))

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Candidate p` = sprintf("%.2f", candidate_p),
  `Probability of exactly 7 heads` = sprintf("%.4f", exp(candidate_loglik)),
  `Relative likelihood` = sprintf("%.3f", candidate_relative),
  check.names = FALSE
))

Among these candidates, (p=0.7) supports the observed result most strongly. A smooth curve shows that it is also the best value among all candidates between 0 and 1.


Show reproducible R code
p_grid <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 1000)
loglik_10 <- dbinom(k, size = n, prob = p_grid, log = TRUE)
relative_10 <- exp(loglik_10 - max(loglik_10))

local({
  old <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1.2, 0.8))
  on.exit(par(old))
  plot(p_grid, relative_10, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#246B8E",
       xlab = "Candidate probability of heads, p",
       ylab = "Relative likelihood", ylim = c(0, 1.04), las = 1)
  abline(v = k / n, lty = 2, col = "#C44E52")
  points(k / n, 1, pch = 19, col = "#C44E52")
  text(k / n, 0.91, expression(hat(p) == 0.7), pos = 4,
       col = "#C44E52")
})








Figure 1: Relative likelihood after observing 7 heads in 10 flips. The curve compares parameter values; it is not a probability density for p.

title: Blog Post 1
section: Why the maximum is the sample proportion
text:
Why the maximum is the sample proportion
Products are easier to differentiate after taking logarithms. Since logarithms are strictly increasing, maximizing (L) is equivalent to maximizing the log-likelihood:

\ell(p)=\log L(p)=\log\binom{n}{k}+k\log p+(n-k)\log(1-p).

For (0<k<n), differentiate and set the score equal to zero:

\ell'(p)=\frac{k}{p}-\frac{n-k}{1-p}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k(1-p)=(n-k)p
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\widehat p=\frac{k}{n}.

This stationary point is the unique maximum because

\ell''(p)=-\frac{k}{p^2}-\frac{n-k}{(1-p)^2}<0
\qquad (0<p<1).

Thus the entire log-likelihood is strictly concave. If (k=0) or (k=n), there is no interior stationary point; the maximum occurs at the boundary, (p=0) or (1). These cases matter because blindly solving a derivative equation would miss them.

title: Blog Post 1
text:
Same estimate, different evidence
Now compare 7 heads in 10 flips with 70 heads in 100 flips. Both give (p=0.7), but the larger experiment should tell us more. Its likelihood curve is much sharper.


Show reproducible R code
relative_likelihood <- function(p, successes, trials) {
  values <- dbinom(successes, size = trials, prob = p, log = TRUE)
  exp(values - max(values))
}

rel_10 <- relative_likelihood(p_grid, 7, 10)
rel_100 <- relative_likelihood(p_grid, 70, 100)

local({
  old <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1.2, 0.8))
  on.exit(par(old))
  plot(p_grid, rel_10, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#D07629",
       xlab = "Candidate probability of heads, p",
       ylab = "Relative likelihood", ylim = c(0, 1.04), las = 1)
  lines(p_grid, rel_100, lwd = 3, col = "#246B8E")
  abline(v = 0.7, lty = 3, col = "grey35")
  legend("topleft", c("7 heads / 10 flips", "70 heads / 100 flips"),
         col = c("#D07629", "#246B8E"), lwd = 3, bty = "n")
})








Figure 2: Both samples have the same maximum-likelihood estimate, but 70 heads in 100 flips produces a more concentrated likelihood.





The connection is mathematical. At the maximum,

-\ell''(\widehat p)=\frac{n}{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)}.

Larger (n) creates greater curvature and a narrower peak. In regular large samples, the inverse curvature gives the approximation

\operatorname{SE}(\widehat p)\approx
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)}{n}}.

It equals about 0.145 for 7/10 and 0.046 for 70/100. This approximation can be poor for small samples or estimates near 0 or 1, so the shape of the likelihood remains informative.

title: Blog Post 1
text:
Assumptions, source, and takeaway
The numbers are constructed for this explanation; no external dataset is used. The binomial model assumes a fixed number of independent flips with one constant (p). Dependence or a changing coin would require a different likelihood. R. A. Fisher’s 1922 paper on the foundations of theoretical statistics helped formalize likelihood as distinct from inverse probability.






NoteTakeaway



Maximum likelihood ranks parameter values by how well they explain fixed, observed data. The maximizer (p=k/n) is a point estimate, not the probability that the parameter is correct. The peak’s width supplies the missing second lesson: two identical estimates can carry very different amounts of information.

title: Education as a Buffer Against Joblessness
text:
A college degree is often discussed as a route to higher pay. But education may also act as insurance against unemployment. This post asks: How has unemployment varied by education since 2000, and who absorbed the largest employment shocks during the Great Recession and COVID-19? The distinction matters for students choosing education, workers considering retraining, and policymakers deciding where recession support should be concentrated.
The answer is not a causal estimate of what a degree does to one individual. Education is related to occupation, age, location, and many other characteristics. Instead, this is a careful description of how labor-market risk is distributed across education groups—and how that distribution changes in a crisis.

text:
A college degree is often discussed as a route to higher pay. But education may also act as insurance against unemployment. This post asks: How has unemployment varied by education since 2000, and who absorbed the largest employment shocks during the Great Recession and COVID-19? The distinction matters for students choosing education, workers considering retraining, and policymakers deciding where recession support should be concentrated.
The answer is not a causal estimate of what a degree does to one individual. Education is related to occupation, age, location, and many other characteristics. Instead, this is a careful description of how labor-market risk is distributed across education groups—and how that distribution changes in a crisis.

title: Education as a Buffer Against Joblessness
text:
Data, definitions, and weights
I use IPUMS Current Population Survey (CPS) basic monthly microdata for every May from 2000 through 2025. Keeping the same calendar month makes the annual comparisons less vulnerable to seasonality. I restrict the sample to civilians ages 25–64: most have completed schooling, and most have not reached conventional retirement age.
Education is grouped into less than high school, high school, some college/associate degree, and bachelor’s degree or higher. Following the official CPS definition, the unemployment rate is
\[
\text{Unemployment rate}=
\frac{\text{unemployed}}{\text{employed}+\text{unemployed}}.
\]
People outside the labor force are therefore absent from this denominator. I examine them separately in the third figure.
Most importantly, every estimate uses WTFINL, the final person-level basic monthly weight. A CPS record does not represent only itself; it represents a different number of people in the U.S. population. Ignoring those weights would describe the downloaded sample rather than the population the survey was designed to measure.


Show reproducible R code
# Core weighting step used inside R/01_analysis.R
unemployment_trend <- cps |>
  filter(in_labor_force) |>
  group_by(year, education) |>
  summarise(
    unemployment_rate = weighted.mean(unemployed, weight),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

title: Education as a Buffer Against Joblessness
text:
A persistent education gradient



Weighted May unemployment rates by education, 2000–2025.


The lines move together over the business cycle, but they rarely cross. In May 2007, before the Great Recession, unemployment was 6.1% for adults without a high-school diploma and 1.9% for college graduates. By May 2010, those rates had reached 14.1% and 4.4%, respectively. Recovery lowered every line, yet it did not erase the gradient.
COVID-19 produced a much sharper one-year spike. Between May 2019 and May 2020, unemployment increased from 4.4% to 18.4% for adults without a high-school diploma, compared with 1.9% to 7.0% for college graduates. Both groups suffered; the size of the shock was highly unequal.

title: Education as a Buffer Against Joblessness
text:
Recessions magnify existing inequality



Unemployment-rate increases during the Great Recession and COVID-19 shock.


The comparison in percentage points makes the pattern clearer. During the Great Recession, the increase ranged from 2.5 points for college graduates to 8.0 points for those without a high-school diploma. During the COVID-19 shock, it ranged from 5.1 to 14.0 points. Jobs held by less-educated workers were more exposed to shutdowns and were often harder to perform remotely, while many college-intensive occupations could continue from home.
This does not mean education fully protected workers. It means that the existing education gap became wider exactly when employment security mattered most.

title: Education as a Buffer Against Joblessness
section: Unemployment is only part of the story
text:
Unemployment is only part of the story



Weighted employment-status composition by education in May 2025.


By May 2025, unemployment had largely retreated, but employment-to-population differences remained. About 84% of working-age college graduates were employed, versus 61% of adults without a high-school diploma. The latter group also had a much larger share outside the labor force: 36% versus 14%. This is why a low unemployment rate alone cannot summarize labor-market attachment.

title: Education as a Buffer Against Joblessness
text:
Takeaway
Education is associated with two forms of labor-market advantage: lower unemployment in normal years and smaller increases during major shocks. The actionable lesson is targeted rather than universal. Recession policy, rapid retraining, and job-search support should reach workers with less education early, because their unemployment rises first and furthest. For individuals, education can be viewed not only as an investment in earnings, but also as partial protection against cyclical job loss.

title: Education as a Buffer Against Joblessness
text:
Reproducibility and source
The complete R script, weighted aggregate tables, and exported figures are available in the project repository. Raw IPUMS microdata are excluded under the IPUMS terms; registered users can reproduce the extract using the documented samples and variables.
